movements.name: Japanese Modernism
movements.summary: Postwar Japan's corporate and national modernism: one bold geometric mark, objective photography, and design built as public infrastructure, crowned by Tokyo 1964.

principles.name: One mark carries the idea
principles.idea: Reduce a nation, event or company to a single geometric statement large enough to fill a poster.

principles.name: Photography as proof of modernity
principles.idea: Use the camera's objectivity and technical difficulty as the message itself.
principles.example: Kamekura and Osamu Hayasaki, Tokyo 1964 sprinter poster, 1962

principles.name: Tradition as geometry
principles.idea: Abstract historical Japanese forms such as Rinpa colour fields, crests and Noh masks into flat geometric elements on a modernist grid.

principles.name: Design as infrastructure
principles.idea: Design is a public system for everyone, including people who cannot read the language.
principles.example: Tokyo 1964 sport pictograms, Yoshiro Yamashita under Masaru Katsumi, 1963

principles.name: The designer as institution-builder
principles.idea: Build shared studios and professional bodies so design can negotiate with industry as an equal.
principles.example: Nippon Design Center, founded by eight companies, 1960

movements.name: Japanese Poster Avant-garde
movements.summary: Tokyo's 1960s underground turned against corporate modernism with dense collage of national symbols, folk motifs, kitsch and fluorescent silkscreen colour.

principles.name: Pastiche as critique
principles.idea: Collage the national symbols modernism suppressed, such as the Rising Sun, Fuji and Hokusai's wave, so they undercut themselves.
principles.example: Tadanori Yokoo, Tadanori Yokoo (Having reached a climax at the age of 29, I was dead), 1965

principles.name: The vernacular is the avant-garde
principles.idea: Bring folk motifs, festival printing and the rural into the city as a political act.
principles.example: Kiyoshi Awazu, art direction for Double Suicide, 1969

principles.name: Maximum density
principles.idea: Fill the sheet and let colour vibrate; refuse white space as an ideology.
principles.example: Tadanori Yokoo, A la Maison de M. Civecawa, 1966

principles.name: The page as a field of energy
principles.idea: Treat covers, books and diagrams as generated patterns and vibrations rather than neutral containers.

principles.name: Politics through affect
principles.idea: Aim the poster at the gut rather than at information.
principles.example: Kiyoshi Awazu, Umi o Kaese (Give Back Our Oceans), 1955

keyWorks.title: Umi o Kaese (Give Back Our Oceans)
A la Maison de M. Civecawa

movements.name: Chinese Modern Design
movements.summary: From Shanghai calendar posters and New Culture covers through the PRC propaganda poster to Hong Kong's cross-cultural identity and contemporary Chinese book design.

principles.name: Commerce as modernity's first language
principles.idea: In China modern visual culture arrived through advertising before it arrived through art schools.
principles.example: Shanghai yuefenpai calendar posters for British American Tobacco and Nanyang Brothers, 1920s-1930s

principles.name: The cover as manifesto
principles.idea: The book jacket was where the New Culture movement looked modern, with abstract motifs and hand-drawn characters.
principles.example: Tao Yuanqing, cover for Lu Xun's Panghuang (Wandering), 1926

principles.name: Satire through the graphic line
principles.idea: Caricature, Deco geometry and photomontage as political commentary under censorship.
principles.example: Zhang Guangyu, Journey to the West caricature cycle, 1945

principles.name: Image as mass mobilisation
principles.idea: One authorised image reproduced without limit, in saturated red with heroic faces and radiant light.
principles.example: Liu Chunhua, Chairman Mao Goes to Anyuan, 1967, reproduced some 900 million times

principles.name: Cross-cultural synthesis
principles.idea: Translate one specific Chinese form into modernist geometry for an international audience, rather than blending cultures into pastiche.
principles.example: Kan Tai-keung, Bank of China symbol, 1980

movements.name: Korean Modern Design
movements.summary: Korea built a design profession from the 1960s and modernised Hangul type, freeing the alphabet's letters from the square syllable block.

principles.name: Liberate the letter from the square
principles.idea: Let each Hangul letter keep one fixed shape so the alphabet's logic shows, instead of distorting letters to fill a square block.

principles.name: The script is the identity
principles.idea: Hangul itself is the most Korean material a designer has, and the national image is built from it.
principles.example: Ahn typeface in the PyeongChang 2018 opening and closing ceremonies

principles.name: Identity as modernisation
principles.idea: Corporate identity introduced as a tool of the export economy and taught to industry by exhibition.
principles.example: Cho Young-jae, DECOMAS exhibition, Shinsegae Gallery, 1976

principles.name: Lyrical illustration as a national voice
principles.idea: A gentle, simplified illustrative style as Korea's counterweight to Swiss objectivity.
principles.example: Kim Kyo-man, culture posters for the 1986 Asian Games and 1988 Olympics

movements.name: Japanese Emptiness
movements.summary: Muji's no-brand design grew into a philosophy of the empty vessel: design that offers space for meaning rather than pushing a message.

principles.name: The empty vessel
principles.idea: Design offers a space each person fills with their own meaning instead of transmitting a message.

principles.name: Subtract the brand
principles.idea: Remove logos, ornament and colour so material and price become the message.
principles.example: Ikko Tanaka, Muji launch packaging in kraft paper and cellophane, 1980

principles.name: White as potential
principles.idea: White is not absence but the state before content.

principles.name: Re-design the ordinary
principles.idea: Look again at everyday objects instead of inventing new ones.
principles.example: Kenya Hara, Re-Design: Daily Products of the 21st Century exhibition, 2000

principles.name: Clarity through organisation
principles.idea: Branding as tidying a client down to one essential form.
principles.example: Kashiwa Sato, Uniqlo identity for the SoHo New York flagship, 2006

keyWorks.title: Re-Design: Daily Products of the 21st Century

movements.name: Superflat
movements.summary: Murakami's theory that Japanese visual culture and postwar society are flat, run as a brand system spanning paintings, merchandise and luxury collaborations.

principles.name: Flatness as cultural theory
principles.idea: No perspective or depth: hard line and flat colour as a claim about a society, not only a style.
principles.example: Takashi Murakami, Superflat exhibition, Parco Gallery, 2000

principles.name: Collapse high and low
principles.idea: Paintings, figures, handbags and album covers treated as one practice.
principles.example: Murakami for Louis Vuitton, Multicolore monogram, 2003

principles.name: The character as brand
principles.idea: A mascot that mutates endlessly across media carries the identity.

principles.name: Cuteness carries trauma
principles.idea: Kawaii surfaces sit over the memory of defeat and the atomic bomb.
principles.example: Murakami, Little Boy exhibition, Japan Society, 2005

keyWorks.title: Little Boy: The Arts of Japan's Exploding Subculture

figures.name: Hiromu Hara
figures.summary: Brought the New Typography to Japan, art-directed FRONT, co-founded the Nippon Design Center and lettered the Tokyo 1964 emblem.

principles.name: Typography serves the client
principles.idea: Designs built logically, without a signature style, on the client's side.
principles.example: Showa Bungaku Zenshu series for Kadokawa, 1952-1955

principles.name: Paper is part of the design
principles.idea: The substrate is designed, not picked from stock.
principles.example: Paper series developed with Takeo, from 1959

principles.name: Modern means, any message
principles.idea: His wartime FRONT shows the New Typography serving propaganda: form does not carry ethics.

figures.name: Yusaku Kamekura
figures.summary: 'The Boss' of postwar Japanese design: Tokyo 1964 emblem and posters, Nikon, NTT, co-founder of NDC and first JAGDA president.

principles.name: Geometry plus light
principles.idea: Pure geometric forms made to glow through colour gradation and photography.

principles.name: Photograph the decisive instant
principles.idea: Build the poster on one technically demanding photograph.

principles.name: The mark as monument
principles.idea: Identities meant to outlast their companies' strategies.

keyWorks.title: Trademarks and Symbols of the World

figures.name: Ikko Tanaka
figures.summary: Rebuilt Rinpa painting from flat geometry, art-directed the Seibu/Saison group's culture and created Muji's no-brand identity.

principles.name: Rinpa from geometry
principles.idea: Rinpa's flat colour fields reconstructed from circles, squares and bands.

principles.name: Design as cultural programming
principles.idea: The art director as curator of a whole culture of shops, theatres and museums.
principles.example: Seibu Museum of Art art direction, 1975-1986

principles.name: The no-brand brand
principles.idea: Remove the logo and let packaging material carry the identity.

figures.name: Kazumasa Nagai
figures.summary: NDC founder member and president, JAGDA's second president, who moved from engraved geometric abstraction to hand-drawn animals.

principles.name: Abstraction as cosmology
principles.idea: Fine engraved line fields that suggest energy and space rather than objects.

principles.name: From abstraction to living creatures
principles.idea: Late work turns to staring animals drawn in ornamental line as a plea for life.

principles.name: The quiet corporate mark
principles.idea: Restrained marks for large institutions.

figures.name: Shigeo Fukuda
figures.summary: 'Japan's Escher': anti-war and environmental posters built on a single visual paradox, and illusion sculptures.

principles.name: One twist does all the work
principles.idea: Reduce the argument to a single impossible image.

principles.name: Figure-ground ambiguity
principles.idea: Two readings in one silhouette.

principles.name: Illusion leaves the page
principles.idea: The same logic built in three dimensions.

figures.name: Kohei Sugiura
figures.role: Graphic and book designer, researcher of Asian iconography
figures.summary: Architect-trained designer who made the book, magazine and diagram serious media in Japan and taught a generation of Asian book designers.

principles.name: Self-proliferating design
principles.idea: One generative pattern re-run through rotations and colours produces a whole series from the same plates.

principles.name: The cover is a face
principles.idea: The cover answers the contents of each issue.
principles.example: Covers for SD and Toshi Jutaku, late 1960s

principles.name: The book as architecture
principles.idea: Design starts from vertical Mincho body text and works outward to the binding.

keyWorks.title: Mandala: Now You See It, Now You Don't

figures.name: Tadanori Yokoo
figures.summary: Collaged the Rising Sun, kitsch and his own biography into psychedelic posters that broke Japanese modernism's consensus.

principles.name: The self as subject
principles.idea: The designer's own biography is the poster's content.

principles.name: Kitsch and sacred side by side
principles.idea: Pin-ups, Buddhist imagery and national symbols in one plane, at equal weight.
principles.example: A la Maison de M. Civecawa, 1966

principles.name: Restless restyling
principles.idea: Refuse a fixed style; deliberately hang incompatible work together.

keyWorks.title: A la Maison de M. Civecawa

figures.name: Kiyoshi Awazu
figures.summary: Self-taught activist designer who designed the Metabolist manifesto and fused folklore, protest and supergraphics.

principles.name: Design sides with the dispossessed
principles.idea: The poster as solidarity with people excluded from power.
principles.example: Umi o Kaese (Give Back Our Oceans), 1955

principles.name: Reproduction as method
principles.idea: Recurring motifs such as fingerprints and turtles reprinted and transformed for decades.
principles.example: A Diversity of Birds, Hiroshima Appeals, 1984

principles.name: Graphics at architectural scale
principles.idea: Supergraphics wrap a whole building.

figures.name: Eiko Ishioka
figures.role: Art director, graphic and costume designer
figures.summary: Parco's art director in the 1970s, then a total designer of film, stage and costume, with an Oscar for Dracula.

principles.name: Advertise an attitude
principles.idea: Sell a stance of independence and eroticism, showing almost no product.

principles.name: Total art direction
principles.idea: Poster, set and costume as one designed world.
principles.example: Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters, 1985

principles.name: Uncompromising originality
principles.idea: Refuse borrowed style; every project from first principles.

keyWorks.title: Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters (production design)

figures.name: Kenya Hara
figures.summary: Muji's art director since 2001 and NDC's president, who theorised emptiness, white and ex-formation as design.

principles.name: Emptiness
principles.idea: Design as an empty vessel that receives meaning rather than sending a message.

principles.name: Ex-formation
principles.idea: Make the familiar unknown again so people notice it, instead of informing them.
principles.example: Ex-formation seminar at Musashino Art University, from 2004

principles.name: Haptic design
principles.idea: Design addressed to touch and the senses before the eye.

keyWorks.title: Re-Design: Daily Products of the 21st Century

figures.name: Kashiwa Sato
figures.summary: Founder of SAMURAI, whose loud reduction in primary colours shaped Uniqlo, Seven-Eleven, Rakuten and the National Art Center, Tokyo.

principles.name: Organising
principles.idea: Branding as tidying: find the essence and discard the rest.

principles.name: Reduction, loudly
principles.idea: Straight lines, primary colours and one strong square.

principles.name: Brand as environment
principles.idea: Logo, store, product and architecture directed as one.

figures.name: Takashi Murakami
figures.summary: Coined Superflat and ran it as a brand system across painting, merchandise, Louis Vuitton and Kanye West covers.

principles.name: The art enterprise
principles.idea: The studio as a company with production lines, like an animation house.

principles.name: Repackage the subcultural
principles.idea: Otaku forms presented as high art and sold back as goods.

principles.name: Curate your own context
principles.idea: Theory, exhibitions and product built together.

figures.name: Zhang Guangyu
figures.summary: Led Shanghai's manhua golden age through Shanghai Sketch and Modern Sketch, fusing Deco, Constructivism and folk art; later designed Havoc in Heaven.

principles.name: Synthesis without hierarchy
principles.idea: Bauhaus, Constructivism, Mexican murals and Chinese folk art in one decorative language.

principles.name: Myth as political weapon
principles.idea: Classical stories retold to satirise the present.
principles.example: Journey to the West caricature cycle, 1945

principles.name: Design across every medium
principles.idea: Furniture, covers, stamps and film from one hand.

figures.name: Qian Juntao
figures.role: Book cover designer, seal carver, calligrapher
figures.summary: Kaiming Bookstore's art editor (1927-1934), nicknamed 'Qian Covers', who made cover design a recognised craft in Republican Shanghai.

principles.name: The seal carver's economy
principles.idea: A carved seal's compression, few strokes in a square field, brought to the cover.

principles.name: Western pattern, Chinese structure
principles.idea: Art Nouveau and Deco ornament for borders and grounds while titles stay hand-drawn Chinese characters.

figures.name: Henry Steiner
figures.summary: Paul Rand's student who arrived in Hong Kong in 1961 and defined cross-cultural corporate identity, from HSBC to Hongkong Land.

principles.name: One element from each side
principles.idea: A Western structure paired with one specific Chinese form, never a pastiche.
principles.example: Hongkong Land H mark with the character for longevity

principles.name: Equity over novelty
principles.idea: Refresh an inherited mark rather than replace it.
principles.example: Hong Kong Jockey Club monogram, redrawn before 1997

principles.name: Banknotes as public storytelling
principles.idea: A currency's imagery as a coherent narrative system.
principles.example: Standard Chartered Hong Kong notes with mythical creatures

figures.name: Kan Tai-keung
figures.summary: Former tailor turned Hong Kong's leading Chinese designer, uniting ink painting with modernist identity, from the Bank of China to Chongqing.

principles.name: Ink as a design element
principles.idea: Literati ink-wash brought into the modernist poster as a pure field of tone.

principles.name: Archaic form, modern geometry
principles.idea: An ancient object redrawn as a modern mark that carries a second reading.

principles.name: The city as a character
principles.idea: A civic identity built from one written character.

figures.name: Alan Chan
figures.role: Graphic and interior designer, brand consultant
figures.summary: Hong Kong brand designer whose 'East meets West' blend of Chinese ornament and Western layout reached Japan and the mainland first.

principles.name: East meets West
principles.idea: Chinese decorative vocabulary set in Western layouts for consumer brands.
principles.example: East Meets West exhibition, Creation Gallery G8, Tokyo, 1991

principles.name: Nostalgia as brand asset
principles.idea: Old Shanghai graphics reissued as products and packaging.
principles.example: Alan Chan Design Company retro products, 1990s

keyWorks.title: Art of Living (Hong Kong Heritage Museum)

figures.name: Lu Jingren
figures.summary: Sugiura-trained Beijing designer who moved Chinese practice from cover decoration to book design as a whole object.

principles.name: Design from the inside out
principles.idea: Text, grid, paper and binding form one structure, starting from the body text.

principles.name: Material as meaning
principles.idea: Wood, thread, rice paper and traditional binding used as structural argument, not decoration.

figures.name: Aaron Nieh
figures.summary: Taiwan's best-known graphic designer: Mandopop packaging, sliced Chinese typography and crowdfunded civic design, first Taiwanese AGI member.

principles.name: Characters as malleable material
principles.idea: Chinese characters sliced, layered and distorted until they are image and text at once.

principles.name: Design as civic action
principles.idea: Crowdfunded political design placed in mass media.

figures.name: Choi Jeong-ho
figures.summary: Drew the myeongjo and gothic Hangul types of the 1950s-60s on which nearly every later Korean text face is based.

principles.name: The text face as infrastructure
principles.idea: Two families, myeongjo and gothic, designed for reading at national scale.

principles.name: Balance inside the square
principles.idea: Each syllable block drawn so its optical colour matches its neighbours across thousands of combinations.

figures.name: Cho Young-jae
figures.summary: Introduced corporate identity to Korea, proposed the first non-square Hangul module, and chaired the Seoul 1988 Olympic design committee.

principles.name: Design as thinking work
principles.idea: The designer as strategist and manager, not decorator.

principles.name: The non-square module
principles.idea: Hangul letters with fixed shapes so machines can set the script beautifully.
principles.example: Paper on Hangul mechanisation, Johyeong no. 1, 1976

figures.name: Ahn Sang-soo
figures.summary: Founder of Ahn Graphics whose 1985 Ahn typeface freed Hangul from the square; Gutenberg Prize 2007 and founder of PaTI.

principles.name: Unlock the square
principles.idea: Fixed-shape letters and the first variable-width Hangul face.

principles.name: Typography as poetry
principles.idea: Letters as a visual score, informed by Yi Sang's typographic poems.
principles.example: Doctoral study of Yi Sang's poetry, 1995

principles.name: Play as pedagogy
principles.idea: Learning by making, outside the official academy.

keyWorks.title: Korean translation of Emil Ruder's Typographie

events.label: Shanghai Sketch launched
events.note: Zhang Guangyu's weekly began Shanghai's manhua golden age, the testing ground for Chinese modernist graphics.

events.label: Nippon Kobo founded
events.note: Natori's studio trained Hiromu Hara and Yusaku Kamekura in modern photo-typographic layout.

events.label: Japan Advertising Artists Club (Nissenbi)
events.note: Japan's first professional body for graphic designers, and its exhibitions launched Awazu, Sugiura and Yokoo.

events.label: Graphic '55 exhibition, Tokyo
events.note: Japanese modernists hung beside Paul Rand at Takashimaya, inspiring the generation that founded NDC.

events.label: PRC newspapers switch to horizontal setting
events.note: On 1 January 1956 every newspaper in the People's Republic moved from vertical to horizontal typesetting by decree.

events.label: World Design Conference, Tokyo
events.note: Held 11-16 May with 227 delegates; it put Japanese design on the world stage and launched the Metabolist manifesto.

events.label: Nippon Design Center opens
events.note: Eight corporations funded a shared design department led by Kamekura, Hara and Tanaka.

events.label: Tokyo 1964 Olympics design programme
events.note: Kamekura's emblem and photo posters and the first systematic Olympic pictograms set the template for event identity.

events.label: Persona exhibition, Matsuya Ginza
events.note: Sixteen young designers, including Yokoo with his hanged self-portrait, announced the break with corporate modernism.

events.label: Cultural Revolution begins
events.note: Propaganda posters reached their peak production and the most centralised image-making in design history.

events.label: Expo '70, Osaka
events.note: Over 64 million visitors; Japanese graphic and architectural avant-gardes worked at national scale on pavilions and signs.

events.label: Korea Society of Graphic Design founded
events.note: Korea's first graphic design association, later KSVD, institutionalised the profession.

events.label: JAGDA founded
events.note: The Japan Graphic Designers Association formed with Kamekura as first president.

events.label: Muji launched
events.note: Forty no-brand products from Seiyu, designed by Ikko Tanaka's team, began the design of emptiness.

events.label: Hiroshima Appeals poster series begins
events.note: JAGDA's annual peace poster, opened by Kamekura's Burning Butterflies, became a lasting commission for Japanese designers.

events.label: Ahn typeface
events.note: The first widely used non-square, variable-width Hangul face, released as a computer font in 1991.

events.label: Seoul Olympics and the horizontal Hankyoreh
events.note: Korea's 1964 moment in design, the same year a national daily launched in horizontal Hangul setting.

events.label: Hong Kong handover
events.note: Colonial identities were renamed and redrawn, and cross-cultural design became Hong Kong's explicit subject.

events.label: Superflat exhibition, Parco Tokyo
events.note: Murakami's show and theory travelled to Los Angeles in 2001, reframing Japanese pop graphics as art.

events.label: Tokyo 2020 pictograms released
events.note: Masaaki Hiromura's team updated the 1964 pictogram heritage, later animated in the 2021 opening ceremony.

events.label: M+ opens in Hong Kong
events.note: Asia's first global museum of visual culture to collect graphic design from across East Asia.
